note: 骨 kuət → kut: default velar onset with the -t coda written — the tightest single syllable in this file. 都 tɑ then begins with the same dental, and step 22 measures what that means: at a junction where a written coda is followed by the same-place onset, the source word carries that consonant once rather than twice in 121 of 140 cases (86%). So 骨都 transcribes kuta, not kutta. 侯 go → -k closes it, a Later Han voiced g- standing for a source k more often than for a source g. kut is “kut, uğur, devlet, baht, talih, saadet” in Kāşgarî — heavenly favour, fortune, sovereign grace — and Clauson records the verb kutad- “to be blessed”, the stem behind the Kutadgu Bilig. Kutak itself is not attested: it would be a deverbal or diminutive formation in -(A)k on that stem, which is a live suffix but not one witnessed on this word. Compare Murad I's Hüdavendigâr and Qutalmış, ancestor of the Seljuks of Rum. Note also that kut is the Turkic candidate for 孤塗, where the Chinese gloss 子 “son” fits the Yeniseian proposal better and not this one.

note: 徑 keŋᶜ → kıng: default velar onset with the -ŋ coda written. 路 lɑᶜ → ra: a Chinese l- for a source r-, which step 15 shows is the ordinary direction — a source r- was written l- in 12 of 14 attestations. The final -k of the Turkic word is not written, and step 20 licenses that: 30% of stop-final source syllables were spelled with an open character. This reading is not the author's. The comparison of 徑路 with Turkic kıŋrak is already in the literature, where it is described as speculative; it entered this project during the corpus build, recorded as cited and unverified. What is new here is that it can be tested, and it survives. Kāşgarî glosses kıñrak as “et ve hamur kesilen satıra benzer büyük bıçak” — a large knife resembling a cleaver — and the Chinese sources independently describe 徑路 as a Xiongnu blade used in oath-taking (the 徑路刀). Two sources with no contact agree about what the object is, which is a stronger kind of agreement than a sound match. A word of identical shape, kañrak “palate”, fits the transcription equally well and is excluded only by the referent. §9.1 of the paper sets this out; the original publication of the comparison still has to be traced.
